You're getting very close. I think you've now understood the role of the ELBO in VAEs, but there's **one important misconception remaining about diffusion models**.

You said:

> Making \(p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\) close to \(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\) is not good enough, because the likelihood of real images involves integrating over all intermediate latent variables.

**The first half is actually sufficient in principle.** If we perfectly learn every reverse transition, and our starting noise distribution matches the forward process's terminal distribution, then we also recover the correct distribution of real images.

The ELBO isn't introduced because matching the reverse transitions is insufficient. It's introduced to give us a principled likelihood-based objective that we can efficiently optimize.

Let me explain why.

## 1. First, a small correction about VAEs

You correctly recalled:

\[
\boxed{
\log p_\theta(x)
=
\mathrm{ELBO}(\theta,\phi)
+
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(
q_\phi(z\mid x)\parallel p_\theta(z\mid x)
\right)
}
\]

However, you said maximizing the ELBO simultaneously increases the likelihood and decreases the KL.

That's the intended effect, but **it isn't mathematically guaranteed that both improve at every optimization step**.

Remember:

\[
\mathrm{ELBO}
=
\log p_\theta(x)-D_{\mathrm{KL}}.
\]

When we update the encoder parameters \(\phi\), holding \(\theta\) fixed, \(\log p_\theta(x)\) is constant.

Therefore:

\[
\max_\phi \mathrm{ELBO}
\iff
\min_\phi D_{\mathrm{KL}}.
\]

But when we update the decoder parameters \(\theta\), both the likelihood and KL can change.

The ELBO encourages a good generative model and a good posterior approximation, without guaranteeing that both improve on every update.

## 2. The likelihood is intractable in both VAE and diffusion

You suggested that the diffusion likelihood is fundamentally more complicated than the VAE likelihood.

It is more computationally demanding because diffusion has many latent variables, but **both have the same underlying mathematical problem**.

For a VAE:

\[
\boxed{
p_\theta(x)
=
\int p(z)p_\theta(x\mid z)\,dz
}
\]

For a diffusion model:

\[
\boxed{
p_\theta(x_0)
=
\int p(x_T)
\prod_{t=1}^{T}
p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
\,dx_{1:T}
}
\]

In both cases, we need to integrate out latent variables.

And in both cases, we can write:

\[
\log p_\theta(\text{data})
=
\mathrm{ELBO}
+
\mathrm{Posterior\ KL}.
\]

The diffusion ELBO is not fundamentally a different variational principle.

It is the same principle applied to a hierarchical latent-variable model.

## 3. Here's the key: perfectly learning the reverse transitions is enough

Imagine we somehow have a perfect neural network:

\[
\boxed{
p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
=
q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
\quad\text{for every }t.
}
\]

Also assume:

\[
p(x_T)=q(x_T).
\]

Now consider the joint distribution generated by our model:

\[
p_\theta(x_{0:T})
=
p(x_T)
\prod_{t=1}^{T}
p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t).
\]

Substitute our assumptions:

\[
\begin{aligned}
p_\theta(x_{0:T})
&=
q(x_T)
\prod_{t=1}^{T}
q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\\
&=q(x_{0:T}).
\end{aligned}
\]

The second equality follows from the reverse factorization of a Markov chain.

Now marginalize all intermediate variables:

\[
\begin{aligned}
p_\theta(x_0)
&=
\int p_\theta(x_{0:T})\,dx_{1:T}\\
&=
\int q(x_{0:T})\,dx_{1:T}\\
&=\boxed{q_{\mathrm{data}}(x_0)}.
\end{aligned}
\]

**We've recovered the actual data distribution!**

So you don't need a separate approximation of the image likelihood once you've correctly learned the entire reverse chain.

The complicated integral still exists, but it doesn't prevent the learned reverse process from generating the correct distribution.

## 4. Why use the ELBO, then?

The reason is to make the learning problem practical and connect it to maximum likelihood.

Your lecture begins on slide 11 with:

\[
\max_\theta\log p_\theta(x_0).
\]

Since this likelihood is intractable, it introduces the ELBO.

The beautiful result is that the expected negative ELBO can be written as:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_{q_{\mathrm{data}}}[-\mathrm{ELBO}]
={}&H(q_{\mathrm{data}})\\
&+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(x_T)\parallel p(x_T))\\
&+\sum_{t=1}^{T}
\mathbb E_{q(x_t)}
\left[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(
q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
\parallel
p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
\right)
\right].
\end{aligned}
}
\]

The first term does not depend on \(\theta\). Neither does the second if the noise prior is fixed.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
\min_\theta\mathbb E[-\mathrm{ELBO}]
\iff
\min_\theta
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
\mathbb E_{q(x_t)}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}
\left(
q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
\parallel
p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
\right).
}
\]

**This is the missing link in your reasoning.**

Maximizing the expected ELBO is equivalent to minimizing the total reverse-transition KL objective, under the assumptions we've been using.

They aren't two separate training problems.

    **Goal**

    Learn to generate real images

    \(p_\theta(x_0)\approx q_{\mathrm{data}}(x_0)\)

  <row justify="center">
    <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/>
  </row>

    Learn every true reverse transition

  </box>
  <row justify="center">
    <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/>
  </row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Training challenge**

    True reverse conditional is intractable to evaluate directly
  </box>
  <row justify="center">
    <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/>
  </row>
  <box background="rgba(12,112,190,0.07)" radius="lg" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Solution**

    Use the ELBO and the exactly known

    \(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\)

    to derive an efficiently computable loss
  </box>
</box>

One extra nuance: you could also optimize the reverse transitions directly using Monte Carlo samples of consecutive forward states, without explicitly deriving the ELBO. The ELBO formulation is especially useful because it makes the connection to data likelihood clear and leads to the analytic Gaussian KL and denoising objectives in your lecture.

You said:

> Making the KL between the true reverse \(q\) and our learned reverse \(p_\theta\) small is not good enough.

I would replace that with:

> **Making all the reverse-transition KL divergences small is precisely what we want. The challenge is obtaining a convenient, computable objective to achieve that. The ELBO gives us such an objective, while also connecting reverse-process learning to maximizing the probability of real images.**

And there's an important distinction between *evaluating* a likelihood and *sampling* from a distribution.

Even if calculating \(p_\theta(x_0)\) involves an intractable integral, we can still generate an \(x_0\) by successively sampling:

\[
x_T\rightarrow x_{T-1}\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow x_0.
\]

We never need to evaluate that enormous integral to generate an image.

That's why diffusion works.

**The central idea:** The reverse model is not merely an approximation that we subsequently need to fix using the ELBO. Learning the reverse model is the goal, and the ELBO is one principled mathematical route to training it.

\log p_\theta(x)
=
\mathrm{ELBO}(\theta,\phi)
+
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(
q_\phi(z\mid x)\parallel p_\theta(z\mid x)
\right)
}
\]

However, you said maximizing the ELBO simultaneously increases the likelihood and decreases the KL.

That's the intended effect, but **it isn't mathematically guaranteed that both improve at every optimization step**\.

Remember\:

\[
\mathrm{ELBO}
=
\log p_\theta(x)-D_{\mathrm{KL}}.
\]

When we update the encoder parameters \(\phi\), holding \(\theta\) fixed, \(\log p_\theta(x)\) is constant.

Therefore\:

\[
\max_\phi \mathrm{ELBO}
\iff
\min_\phi D_{\mathrm{KL}}.
\]

But when we update the decoder parameters \(\theta\), both the likelihood and KL can change.

The ELBO encourages a good generative model and a good posterior approximation, without guaranteeing that both improve on every update.

## 2\. The likelihood is intractable in both VAE and diffusion

You suggested that the diffusion likelihood is fundamentally more complicated than the VAE likelihood.

It is more computationally demanding because diffusion has many latent variables, but **both have the same underlying mathematical problem**\.

For a VAE\:

\[
\boxed{
p_\theta(x)
=
\int p(z)p_\theta(x\mid z)\,dz
}
\]

For a diffusion model\:

\[
\boxed{
p_\theta(x_0)
=
\int p(x_T)
\prod_{t=1}^{T}
p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
\,dx_{1:T}
}
\]

In both cases, we need to integrate out latent variables.

And in both cases, we can write\:

\[
\log p_\theta(\text{data})
=
\mathrm{ELBO}
+
\mathrm{Posterior\ KL}.
\]

The diffusion ELBO is not fundamentally a different variational principle.

It is the same principle applied to a hierarchical latent-variable model.

## 3\. Here's the key: perfectly learning the reverse transitions is enough

Imagine we somehow have a perfect neural network\:

\[
\boxed{
p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
=
q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
\quad\text{for every }t.
}
\]

Also assume\:

\[
p(x_T)=q(x_T).
\]

Now consider the joint distribution generated by our model\:

\[
p_\theta(x_{0:T})
=
p(x_T)
\prod_{t=1}^{T}
p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t).
\]

Substitute our assumptions\:

\[
\begin{aligned}
p_\theta(x_{0:T})
&=
q(x_T)
\prod_{t=1}^{T}
q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\\
&=q(x_{0:T}).
\end{aligned}
\]

The second equality follows from the reverse factorization of a Markov chain.

Now marginalize all intermediate variables\:

\[
\begin{aligned}
p_\theta(x_0)
&=
\int p_\theta(x_{0:T})\,dx_{1:T}\\
&=
\int q(x_{0:T})\,dx_{1:T}\\
&=\boxed{q_{\mathrm{data}}(x_0)}.
\end{aligned}
\]

**We've recovered the actual data distribution\!**

So you don't need a separate approximation of the image likelihood once you've correctly learned the entire reverse chain.

The complicated integral still exists, but it doesn't prevent the learned reverse process from generating the correct distribution.

## 4\. Why use the ELBO, then?

The reason is to make the learning problem practical and connect it to maximum likelihood.

Your lecture begins on slide 11 with\:

\[
\max_\theta\log p_\theta(x_0).
\]

Since this likelihood is intractable, it introduces the ELBO.

The beautiful result is that the expected negative ELBO can be written as\:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_{q_{\mathrm{data}}}[-\mathrm{ELBO}]
={}&H(q_{\mathrm{data}})\\
&+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(x_T)\parallel p(x_T))\\
&+\sum_{t=1}^{T}
\mathbb E_{q(x_t)}
\left[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(
q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
\parallel
p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
\right)
\right].
\end{aligned}
}
\]

The first term does not depend on \(\theta\)\. Neither does the second if the noise prior is fixed.

Therefore\:

\[
\boxed{
\min_\theta\mathbb E[-\mathrm{ELBO}]
\iff
\min_\theta
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
\mathbb E_{q(x_t)}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}
\left(
q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
\parallel
p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
\right).
}
\]

**This is the missing link in your reasoning.**

Maximizing the expected ELBO is equivalent to minimizing the total reverse-transition KL objective, under the assumptions we've been using.

They aren't two separate training problems.

## 5\. So the actual logic is this

**Goal**

Learn to generate real images

\(p_\theta(x_0)\approx q_{\mathrm{data}}(x_0)\)

**Sufficient strategy**

Learn every true reverse transition

\(p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\approx q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\)

**Training challenge**

True reverse conditional is intractable to evaluate directly

**Solution**

Use the ELBO and the exactly known

\(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\)

to derive an efficiently computable loss

One extra nuance: you could also optimize the reverse transitions directly using Monte Carlo samples of consecutive forward states, without explicitly deriving the ELBO. The ELBO formulation is especially useful because it makes the connection to data likelihood clear and leads to the analytic Gaussian KL and denoising objectives in your lecture.

You said\:

> Making the KL between the true reverse \(q\) and our learned reverse \(p_\theta\) small is not good enough.

I would replace that with\:

> **Making all the reverse-transition KL divergences small is precisely what we want. The challenge is obtaining a convenient, computable objective to achieve that. The ELBO gives us such an objective, while also connecting reverse-process learning to maximizing the probability of real images.**

And there's an important distinction between *evaluating* a likelihood and *sampling* from a distribution.

Even if calculating \(p_\theta(x_0)\) involves an intractable integral, we can still generate an \(x_0\) by successively sampling\:

\[
x_T\rightarrow x_{T-1}\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow x_0.
\]

We never need to evaluate that enormous integral to generate an image.

That's why diffusion works.

**The central idea\:** The reverse model is not merely an approximation that we subsequently need to fix using the ELBO. Learning the reverse model is the goal, and the ELBO is one principled mathematical route to training it.
